detailed_description: The Byte Counter tool provides precise byte measurement for text across multiple character encodings (UTF-8, UTF-16LE, UTF-16BE, and ASCII). This tool calculates byte length by converting input text into the selected encoding's binary representation, accounting for encoding-specific mechanics like Unicode code point transformations and endianness in UTF-16 variants. For UTF-8, it applies RFC 3629-compliant encoding rules where characters from U+0000 to U+10FFFF occupy 1-4 bytes. UTF-16 calculations handle surrogate pairs (0xD800-0xDFFF) correctly, using 4 bytes for code points beyond U+FFFF. ASCII mode strictly measures 7-bit characters at 1 byte each, truncating extended ASCII values. Developers working with constrained memory environments, network protocols requiring exact byte counts, or file format specifications (e.g., FITS headers with 80-byte records) will find this tool essential for verifying text payloads. The algorithm operates client-side using JavaScript's TextEncoder API for accurate browser-based encoding simulation, displaying real-time hexadecimal byte representations for educational purposes.
usage_steps: Type or paste text into the primary input text area with line wrapping enabled
Select target encoding from the dropdown menu (UTF-8, UTF-16LE, UTF-16BE, ASCII)
Observe the calculated byte count displayed in the status panel with precision to individual bytes
Toggle the 'Show Hex' switch to visualize the hexadecimal representation of encoded bytes
Click the 'Copy Hex' button to copy the byte sequence for debugging in hex editors or packet analyzers
Use the 'Reset' button to clear input and start fresh while preserving encoding selection
usage_examples: A firmware engineer verifying string resources fit within a 256-byte EEPROM allocation using UTF-16LE encoding
A web developer optimizing JSON API payloads to stay under HTTP/2 frame size limits (typically 16KB)
A data scientist preparing UTF-8 encoded CSV files that must not exceed 1,048,576 bytes for legacy system ingestion
A security analyst comparing ASCII vs UTF-8 byte counts to detect potential encoding-based obfuscation in log entries
